prompt:
A 66-year-old man had a drug-eluting stent placed in his proximal LAD 10 weeks ago for an NSTEMI. He has type 2 diabetes, a prior TIA, and stage 3a CKD. He takes aspirin 81 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, metoprolol succinate, and empagliflozin. He has a symptomatic but easily reducible inguinal hernia, and the surgeon wants to repair it next week. The surgeon has asked us to stop both antiplatelets 7 days beforehand and 'bridge with Lovenox.' He has no cardiac symptoms, walks 2 miles daily, and his post-MI echo showed an EF of 50%. What preoperative evaluation and recommendations do you suggest?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Recommend postponing the elective hernia repair until dual antiplatelet therapy can be safely shortened, ideally 12 months and at minimum 6 months after PCI for acute coronary syndrome.
Advise against stopping ticagrelor now because stent thrombosis risk is highest in the early months after PCI for acute coronary syndrome.
Continue aspirin without interruption through the eventual surgery unless the surgeon judges bleeding risk prohibitive.
Talk directly with the surgeon and the interventional cardiologist to agree on the timing and antiplatelet plan.
Ask the surgeon whether there is any incarceration, obstruction, or strangulation concern that would make the repair urgent.
Teach the patient hernia warning signs, such as irreducibility, severe pain, vomiting, or skin changes, and to seek emergency care if they occur.
If surgery cannot be deferred, hold ticagrelor for about 3-5 days rather than 7, continue aspirin, and resume ticagrelor within 24-48 hours after hemostasis.
Document that his functional capacity is above 4 METs and that no preoperative stress testing is indicated.
Continue the beta-blocker through the perioperative period.
Hold empagliflozin for about 3 days before surgery because of euglycemic ketoacidosis risk.
Tell the patient in writing never to stop either antiplatelet agent without speaking to his cardiologist.
Plan to reevaluate at 6-12 months after PCI to schedule the repair once ticagrelor can be discontinued.
Continue high-intensity statin therapy perioperatively.
Estimate perioperative cardiac risk with a validated tool such as the Revised Cardiac Risk Index.
Obtain a preoperative ECG given known coronary disease.
Check baseline creatinine, complete blood count, and glucose control before surgery.
If surgery must happen early, do it at a hospital with on-site PCI capability.
Plan postoperative ischemia surveillance, including troponin testing if symptoms or hemodynamic changes occur.
Offer interim hernia symptom measures, such as activity modification, while surgery is deferred.
Reinforce secondary prevention, including glycemic and blood pressure control and tobacco avoidance.
Stop both aspirin and ticagrelor 7 days before surgery next week.
Bridge the antiplatelet interruption with enoxaparin as protection against stent thrombosis.
Switch ticagrelor to prasugrel before surgery.
Plan spinal or epidural anesthesia without holding ticagrelor for the recommended interval.
Refuse surgery even if the hernia becomes incarcerated because he is on dual antiplatelet therapy.
Tell the surgeon that a low-risk operation makes antiplatelet interruption safe at any time after PCI.
Order a pharmacologic stress test before the hernia repair despite good functional capacity.
Refer for repeat coronary angiography before surgery in the absence of symptoms.
Stop the beta-blocker the day before surgery.
Delay restarting antiplatelet therapy for 1-2 weeks after surgery.
Increase aspirin to 325 mg daily while he continues ticagrelor.
Tell the patient he may stop his antiplatelets on his own if he notices bruising.
Prescribe ketorolac or another NSAID for postoperative pain.
Order a routine preoperative echocardiogram.
Order preoperative coronary CT angiography.
Stop atorvastatin before surgery.
Continue empagliflozin through the morning of surgery.
Give prophylactic platelet transfusion before surgery.
Order carotid ultrasound before surgery for a remote TIA without new neurologic symptoms.
Use routine platelet function testing to decide when surgery can proceed.
